1#א: And it was mixed. The Taz wrote: and if that mixture was mixed again in a second mixture, he wrote below siman 110 seif 8 that it is permitted. The Shach wrote that even in two mixtures it is forbidden in something that has a permitted aspect.
1#ב: In what is not its kind. The Shach wrote: it appears that here we follow the name and not the taste — if it is equal in name, even though not equal in taste, it is its kind and is not nullified; and if it is not equal in name, even though equal in taste, it is not its kind and is nullified.
1#ג: To whiten it. Since it is for appearance it is not nullified, as stated in Orach Chayim siman 513 seif 3 — see there. And when placing it in a pot to fix — Maharai's reason: everything placed one in another to fix is called its kind, like water and salt in dough, which is considered its kind since they fix the dough. The Taz wrote: one should not err from this regarding what we say in many places that one against two is nullified in its kind from the Torah, and not in its kind requires sixty from the Torah — to say that there too it is its kind when it fixes the pot as here, for there the law depends on taste since taste in not its kind, and this taste in the pot automatically has a stringent name as not its kind.
2#א: In the future. Such as an egg laid on Yom Tov that will certainly be permitted after Yom Tov — unlike a doubtful tereifah egg cited afterward.
2#ב: Doubt. Maharam Mintz challenged: why did the Mechaber write "because the permitting matter is not certain" — this law of doubtful tereifah does not apply to something that has a permitted aspect at all; for regarding an egg laid on Yom Tov it is properly called something that has a permitted aspect, for now it is forbidden and tomorrow it will be permitted — unlike a doubtful tereifah egg: even if permission is in his hand or will certainly come, nevertheless if mixed with others it should be nullified — if the chicken is tereifah the egg should be nullified; if kosher, the egg was never forbidden and something that has a permitted aspect applies only if now forbidden and later permitted. It appears the Mechaber deals with a doubtful tereifah egg also laid on Yom Tov — even if the chicken is later kosher, today the egg is forbidden because it was laid on Yom Tov; one might think if that egg mixed on Yom Tov it would not be nullified in a thousand lest the chicken be kosher and there is no prohibition — it teaches that since the permitting matter is not certain to come, perhaps it is tereifah, it is not called something that has a permitted aspect and is nullified — investigate.
3#_: Outlay. The Shach wrote that Maharil disagrees, for kashering outlay is a small matter; proof from maaser sheni that is something that has a permitted aspect through bringing up to Jerusalem, etc. — see there. One should be concerned for his words where there is no great loss; and it appears one should wait until the vessels are not ben yomo, then they are permitted from the Torah, but each alone is forbidden to use until after twelve months — for the Tur did not write that it is not something that has a permitted aspect only because outlay is required; when there is Torah permission without any outlay, all forbid. Ben Lev ruled a dairy bowl mixed with meat bowls is not nullified in the majority since not in its kind — all forbidden; the Bach seized on this and was stringent to remove one vessel as a mere stringency like Maharam with meat pieces — but all poskim agreed in siman 109 that one need not remove even a piece; Maharam did so because he was righteous and feared eating prohibition disgracefully, etc. — not applicable to vessels. Nevertheless, without loss, be stringent like the Bach; see siman 69 seif 10. The Taz also ruled one may kasher all vessels — see there.
4#א: Its taste. The Taz explained: if the prohibition was removed and only taste was emitted, that taste is not stringent to forbid on account of something that has a permitted aspect. And it is not like seif 1 placing an egg in a pot to fix — there the egg is for the taste of the dish — so Beit Yosef in Orach Chayim siman 513. However the Shach disagrees and wrote that for practical law it appears even if the whole taste was emitted it is not nullified; and Bach wrote similarly.
4#ב: Itself. The Shach wrote: all poskim seized on the Rav in this, for something that has a permitted aspect — what difference if absorbed or not, ultimately there is permission for its prohibition.
4#ג: Some say. Meaning: and the main opinion is not so — it is not called something that has a permitted aspect since for roasting it was never forbidden, as stated in siman 69.
4#ד: The absorbed. The Taz challenged: why did the Rama need a reason about vessels because of outlay, and not say the reason is absorbed prohibition? Answer: for vessels it is also because of absorption, but the Rama wrote outlay to teach elsewhere where outlay is required it is not something that has a permitted aspect. What is different from wine that fell in a barrel of one who vowed — that is something that has a permitted aspect, for there it is not absorption but mixture and the substance of the prohibition is there? Nevertheless in the main law he agrees with the Shach that there is no distinction for something that has a permitted aspect between absorbed taste or substance — none are nullified. But what he wrote that an unsalted piece is also something that has a permitted aspect is not as he wrote in s.k. 9.
4#ה: Before. The Shach explained: e.g. a barrel full of grapes in clusters with much clear wine before Shabbat — one may take wine on Shabbat even though more drips constantly, for it is nullified in what already exited and there is no something that has a permitted aspect since wine was never recognizable by itself; likewise a barrel of whole grapes filled with water for tamad — grapes burst later and all wine exits — one may draw on Shabbat to drink, for the little wine exiting on Shabbat mixes and nullifies in existing wine that was never once recognizable alone — and similarly — end of his words.
4#ו: Disagree. The Shach in Torat Chatat ruled like the first reason; Maharshal disagreed. The two reasons the Mechaber brought in Orach Chayim siman 447 — one can say they also disagree whether chametz is something that has a permitted aspect.
4#ז: One who cooks. And as explained in Orach Chayim siman 318.
